---
title: "Agentic coding: build a clinical tool in an hour, then find what is wrong with it"
subtitle: "About 85 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** A chatbot can now build a working clinical calculator from a
  plain request in about ten minutes. The arithmetic is usually right. The
  skill that matters is checking the rest: its rules, its edge cases, and
  which version of the score it uses, against the original paper and MDCalc.
- **What you do.** Build a calculator for a score from your specialty, then
  run three made-up patients through it, MDCalc, and the paper.
- **What you keep.** Your tool, and a table of three checked cases with the
  one change you would make before anyone else used it.
- **Short on time?** Do Parts A and B of the Do first (about an hour).
  Then read "Three ways the tool you just built can be wrong".
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Say what a coding agent does that a chatbot does not, and why that changes
   who is responsible for checking the result.
2. Build a working single-page clinical calculator from a plain-language
   prompt, in a browser, with no install.
3. Check your tool against the original publication and MDCalc on three
   made-up cases, including an edge case, and say where it agrees and where it
   does not.
4. Explain why your tool is a study aid, and name what would have to change
   before anyone relied on it.

Course competencies: AIM-5 (clinical use), AIM-2 (critical appraisal), AIM-4
(ethics, law, and regulation).
:::

**What you need.** Your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account, and one
tab open on MDCalc, the free calculator website most residents use. Nothing to
install. Made-up patients only. The Do takes about an hour; the video is
optional.

**Build first if you like.** The Do works without the reading. Go to [Part A
of the Do](#build-it), build your tool, then come back and read while you
check it.

## The spreadsheet on the shared drive

Fourth month of intern year, hepatology service. The second-year resident on
your team built a web page over a weekend. You paste in five lab values. It
gives you a MELD-Na score, which estimates how likely a patient with liver
disease is to die in the next three months. It also tells you whether the
patient has reached the team's threshold for a transplant referral.
It is bookmarked on every workroom computer. The attending mentioned it on
rounds as an example of initiative. Everyone uses it, and you have used it
twice today.

This morning the transplant coordinator calls about a patient with a
creatinine of 1.6 who has been on dialysis since Tuesday. The team's number
for her is 24. The coordinator's number is 32. Eight points is the difference
between waiting and being referred this week. The coordinator wants to know
where 24 came from.

::: {.app-mock}
<div class="bar">⬤ ⬤ ⬤ &nbsp; teamtools.local/meld &nbsp;·&nbsp; MELD-Na quick calc</div>
<div class="body">
<h4>MELD-Na</h4>
<div class="row"><span>Bilirubin (mg/dL)</span><span>3.4</span></div>
<div class="row"><span>INR</span><span>1.9</span></div>
<div class="row flag"><span>Creatinine (mg/dL)</span><span>1.6</span></div>
<div class="row"><span>Sodium (mmol/L)</span><span>134</span></div>
<div class="row flag"><span>Dialysis ≥2× this week</span><span>(no field)</span></div>
<div class="score"><b>24</b><span>MELD-Na · below referral threshold</span></div>
</div>
<div class="banner">Built with ChatGPT · for team use</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative tool for this chapter, drawn in CSS; not a real product. The highlighted rows are where the two numbers part company.</div>
:::

Look at the tool before reading on. It has no place to say the patient is on
dialysis. That is not a bug in the arithmetic. The formula the resident asked
for was built exactly as described. What the description left out was a rule
the transplant system attached to the formula. When a patient has had dialysis
twice in the past week, creatinine is set to 4.0 before it enters the
equation, whatever the lab says. Apply that rule to this patient and the score
moves from 24 to 32. The coordinator is right. (The tool also accepts a sodium
of 118 without comment, though the score's rules limit sodium to 125 at the
lowest. That rule did not matter for this patient. It will for the next one.)

Nobody lied. Nobody was careless in the ordinary sense. The tool worked
perfectly for the first thirty patients, none of whom were on dialysis. The
resident asked a language model for a MELD-Na calculator and got one. What
the resident did not do was ask what the score's rules say happens at the edges. And
nobody on the team, including you, checked. The patient does not know the
project exists. Because of a number from a weekend project, she would have
waited.

This chapter is about building a tool like that yourself, in about ten
minutes, and then spending half an hour checking it. The build is the easy
part now. The checking is the skill.

## Why this matters

You will see a tool like the resident's within the year. They are cheap to
make, and every team has someone who makes them. More and more, they are
built by describing what you want to a model and accepting what comes back.
That part now works: in a three-hour workshop, all three groups of medical
students built a working health app by prompting [@pmid:42394077]. The person
who built it is usually proud of it. The attending is usually pleased. Nobody
has been asked to check it, because checking a colleague's tool is not a job
anyone is assigned.

In intern year you will be the intern with the bookmark, or the intern who
built it. Either way the skill you need is the same. Take a tool that seems to
work, decide what it would take to trust it, and go and look.

## How it works

### A chatbot answers; an agent acts

Everything you have used so far in this course is a chatbot. You type, it
writes, you copy what you want out of the reply. A **coding agent** is the same
kind of model wrapped in a loop. It plans a step. It takes an action in the
world: writes a file, runs a program, reads the output. It looks at what
happened, and plans the next step. The actions are real. Files change, code
runs. Because the actions are real, agents run with **permissions**, a list of
what they are allowed to touch. @fig-chatbot-agent shows the two shapes.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-chatbot-agent
%%| fig-cap: "Two ways to use the same model. A chatbot writes text and stops. A coding agent loops: plan, act on real files or programs, observe the result, and continue, inside a boundary of permissions you set."
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart with two boxes. Left, Chatbot: your prompt leads to the model writing text, then to you copying what you want. Right, Coding agent: your goal leads to plan a step, then act by writing a file or running code, then observe the result, which loops back to plan a step or ends by showing you what it built."
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Two ways to use the same model
  accDescr: Flowchart with two boxes. Left, Chatbot, your prompt leads to the model writing text, then to you copying what you want. Right, Coding agent, your goal leads to plan a step, then act by writing a file or running code, then observe the result, which loops back to plan a step or ends by showing you what it built.
  subgraph C["Chatbot"]
    direction TB
    p1[Your prompt] --> t1[Model writes text]
    t1 --> u1[You copy what you want]
  end
  subgraph A["Coding agent"]
    direction TB
    p2[Your goal] --> plan[Plan a step]
    plan --> act[Act: write a file, run code]
    act --> obs[Observe the result]
    obs --> plan
    obs --> done[Show you what it built]
  end
```

The tools you will use today are somewhere between the two. Your chatbot opens a side
panel, writes a web page into it, and shows you the running page. That is the
smallest possible version of the loop: the model wrote a file and the browser
ran it. You are the one watching the result. The full agents work inside a
folder of files on your own computer. They are mentioned at the end
of the chapter and are not used here on purpose. They need an install and a
terminal, and neither is the point.

The point is what changes when the output is something that *runs*. A wrong
sentence in a chatbot reply sits there until you read it. A wrong rule in a
calculator does its work silently, on every patient, until somebody compares
its answer to another source. The error comes from the same place as in
[the critical appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd): the model writes
plausible text, here plausible code, unless it is given a source to check
against. But now the error sits inside a tool that runs on every patient,
where nobody reads it.

A useful way to think of the model is as a capable but junior colleague. It
is fast, fluent, and willing, and it needs clear instructions and review.
Review its work the way a senior reviews a junior's. Do not trust the
confident tone; check the parts that would hurt someone if wrong.

### Three ways the tool you just built can be wrong

A generated calculator can fail in three ways, and each can happen on its own.
Each has a matching check in the Do block.

| Failure | What it looks like | How you catch it |
|---|---|---|
| **The rule** | A point value, cutoff, or coefficient is wrong, or a rule that comes with the score is missing (the dialysis rule; the sodium limits; whether a score is only applied above a threshold) | Compare every rule to the original publication, not to your memory of it |
| **The edge** | The tool does something the builder never imagined, for inputs the builder never tried: nothing checked, two boxes checked that cannot both be true, a value outside the range the score was built on | Try the inputs the builder did not: empty, contradictory, extreme |
| **The version** | The score has more than one published form, and the tool does not say which one it uses (Wells' criteria exist in a three-tier and a two-tier form; the transplant system replaced MELD-Na with MELD 3.0 in 2023) | Ask which version, and check that against what your team, and MDCalc, actually use |

: Three independent failures. A tool can pass two and fail the third. {#tbl-tool-failures}

The first row is where the evidence is clearest. In late 2023, researchers
gave ChatGPT 48 kinds of medical calculation. It got about one answer in three
wrong, even though it could already write and run its own code
[@pmid:40097720]. More than half of its mistakes were in the rules: the wrong
points for an item, or an item missed or made up. On the ten hardest
calculations, with new test cases and a newer model, the team then tested what
helps. Letting the model write and run code helped only a little: wrong
answers fell from about 64 to 54 percent. Giving it MDCalc's written
instructions helped much more. Giving it calculators that people had built
and checked, which it could call, cut wrong answers to 4.8 percent.

So writing code does not make a model reliable. Rules from a checked source
do. Your tool will usually do its arithmetic correctly. But its rules are only
as good as the model's memory of the score, and a rule it leaves out leaves no
trace. That is why you check it against MDCalc and the paper.

The second row is where non-programmers are weakest: they test the cases they
thought of. The medical students whose apps all worked added no protection for
the data the apps collected. The authors concluded that easier building has
to come with training in data security [@pmid:42394077]. An editorial in
the laboratory medicine literature gives the pattern a name you will recognise
from the wards, the illusion of competence. Code that is correctly written and
looks professional is most convincing to the people least able to find its
flaws. There is a real difference between code that runs and code that is
safe to run on patients [@pmid:42695169].

A tool that is mostly right is the hardest case. A nursing research group used
a coding agent to run a statistical analysis (a logistic regression) and
compared its output with a published reference. The coefficients and *p*
values matched. An error in one confidence interval was missed on the first
review and found only later [@pmid:42611917]. The tool was mostly right, which
is the condition under which people stop checking.

### What "checked" looks like

The counterexample is worth knowing because it shows the standard can be met. A
cardiology group built a web calculator for three acute coronary syndrome risk
scores, with ChatGPT writing the code. They then compared its output against
226 registry patients whose scores had been computed independently. They
report complete agreement (*r* = 1.000 for both scores that had a registry
comparison), with the registry named [@pmid:40462782]. That is not a large
study. It is not clinical validation either, which would mean showing the tool
helps patients; the authors say that further clinical validation is needed.
It is what a *technical* check looks like: an outside source of truth, a fixed
set of cases, and a written result.

The resident's tool in the workroom had none of those. Yours, in half an hour,
will have a small version of all three.

### Four questions before anyone else uses it

A 2026 framework for software that clinicians build this way names the main
hazard *comprehension abdication* [@pmid:42564266]. It means handing your
understanding over to the tool that wrote the code, so that you cannot say
what it does for every input. The framework rates a tool's risk with four
questions: does it touch patient data, does its output inform a treatment
decision, can the person using it check the output, and does it reach one
person or a whole institution?

### Where a toy becomes a device

**Toy, not device.** Your tool carries a banner saying so, written into the
prompt before the tool exists. If a page like this is ever used for real care,
it may count as a regulated medical device, which [the ethics
chapter](core-ethics-regulation.qmd) covers. Either way, a score in your note
is yours: record where it came from, and make that the paper or MDCalc.

## Watch or listen (optional)

**Video.** Andrej Karpathy, *Software Is Changing (Again)*, keynote at Y
Combinator's AI Startup School, San Francisco, 17 June 2025 (published 19 June
2025; 39 min). <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ>. YouTube's
captions are automatic and adequate.

Fifteen minutes is enough: skip the opening on "Software 3.0" and go to the
middle third. There he describes *partial autonomy* apps and the *autonomy
slider*. The useful question about an AI tool is not whether it is
autonomous. It is how much freedom you have given it for this task, and how
fast you can check what it did. For the tool you are about to build, ask
where that setting is, and who checks the result.

**Instead, or as well.** The author's slides, [From Chatbots to Coding
Agents](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-06-18-cshl/) (June 2026), go through
the plan-act-observe loop in @fig-chatbot-agent with examples. A [recording
from October 2025](https://talks.seandavis.net/2025-10-17-idpt-vibe-coding/),
from this course's predecessor, shows a calculator being built in front of a
class, with the mistakes left in.

## Do

**Made-up patients only.** [What counts as patient
information](../course/patient-information.qmd). Every number you type is one
you invented: if a test case needs a sodium of 118, invent a patient with a
sodium of 118. Put nothing in your page worth stealing: no passwords, no
names, no real data.

::: {.callout-tip title="Which tool"}
**ChatGPT Edu (your university account).** Ask for the page and it should
open in the *canvas* side panel, which shows the page you built, running,
with a preview button. If canvas does not appear, your workspace may have
canvas code turned off; use the fallback below.^[[VERIFY: run the starter prompt in the CU ChatGPT Edu workspace with a university login and confirm the canvas preview appears; OpenAI's admin documentation says canvas code execution is a workspace setting, checked 2026-09-08]{.verify}]

**Fallback, which also works in Copilot.** Ask for "a single HTML file". Copy
the whole code block into a plain text editor (Notepad, or TextEdit in
plain-text mode). Save it as `calc.html` and double-click it. Your browser
opens it. Nothing is installed. You have made a file, which is what an agent
would have done for you.
:::

### Part A: build it (20 minutes) {#build-it}

**Step 1. Pick a score.** Choose the one closest to your specialty from
@tbl-menu. Each has an original publication you will check against, and
each has at least one edge the model tends to miss. If none fits, use
CHA₂DS₂-VASc; it is the one the worked example below is written for.

| Specialty | Score | Original publication | Where the edges are |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medicine, cardiology, neurology | CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in atrial fibrillation) | Lip et al., *Chest* 2010 [@pmid:19762550] | Two age bands that cannot both be true at once; the "female sex" point, which some current guidelines no longer score; the annual stroke-risk percentages come from a *different* paper [@pmid:22246443] |
| Emergency medicine | Wells' criteria for pulmonary embolism | Wells et al., *Thromb Haemost* 2000 [@pmid:10744147] | Half-point items and rounding; a three-tier and a two-tier version with different cutoffs; "PE is the most likely diagnosis" is a judgment, not a finding |
| Surgery, gastroenterology, transplant | MELD-Na | Kim et al., *NEJM* 2008 [@pmid:18768945]; MELD itself, Kamath et al., *Hepatology* 2001 [@pmid:11172350]; the US transplant system's rules for both, set out in Kim et al., *Gastroenterology* 2021 [@pmid:34481845] | Values below 1.0 are set to 1.0; creatinine capped at 4.0 and set to 4.0 with dialysis; the 2008 paper limits sodium to 125–140, the transplant system to 125–137, and adds the sodium term only when MELD is above 11; MELD 3.0 replaced MELD-Na on the national waiting list in 2023 |
| Critical care, emergency medicine | qSOFA | Seymour et al., *JAMA* 2016 [@pmid:26903335] | The Glasgow Coma Scale cutoff (any score below 15, not a lower threshold); the systolic pressure boundary is ≤100, not <100; what the score is *for* (screening outside the ICU, not diagnosis) |
| Psychiatry, primary care, pediatrics | PHQ-9 | Kroenke et al., *J Gen Intern Med* 2001 [@pmid:11556941] | Nine items scored 0–3 and the severity bands between them; item 9, on self-harm, needs a response the calculator should not leave to a colour |
| Radiology | Fleischner 2017 incidental pulmonary nodule follow-up | MacMahon et al., *Radiology* 2017 [@pmid:28240562] | A decision table, not a sum: solid versus subsolid, single versus multiple, size bands, and a risk category; the guideline explicitly excludes several populations, and the tool will not know that unless told |

: The menu. Every publication was checked in PubMed for this chapter; the edges column is where to look first in Part B. {#tbl-menu}

**Step 2. Paste the starter prompt**, with your score substituted, into a
fresh conversation. Use it word for word the first time. The safety wording is
inside it on purpose. What comes back depends on how the request is phrased,
and the same prompt produces different code on different days. Using the
fixed text means your result reflects the model, not how fluently you write
prompts. If English is not your first language, that is the point.

> Build a single-page web app, as one self-contained HTML file, that
> calculates the `<score>`. Show each input as a checkbox or numeric field
> with its point value or coefficient visible. Display the running total and
> the interpretation the original publication attaches to it. Add a prominent
> red banner: "Educational prototype only. Not validated for clinical
> decision-making." In a footnote, cite the original publication for the
> score and say exactly which version of the score you implemented, so I can
> independently verify every rule against MDCalc and the paper before I trust
> the output. Open it in canvas so I can preview it.

**Step 3. Ask for two changes.** Whatever comes back, ask for two changes, one
at a time. Watch what the model does to the rest of the page each time:

- "Colour the interpretation by risk tier."
- "Add a 'clear all' button, and tell me what the score shows when nothing is
  entered."

The second request is really a check, phrased as a feature. Read the answer.

You now have a working tool. It took about ten minutes, and it probably looks
better than the resident's. Do not share it yet.

### Part B: break it (30 minutes)

Open MDCalc and the original paper from @tbl-menu side by side with your tool.
Run three invented cases through all three sources and record the results in
the template below.

**Case 1, ordinary.** A patient clearly inside the population the score was
made for, with nothing unusual. All three should agree, and usually will. If
they do not, you have found a rule error. Note it and continue.

**Case 2, the edge.** Take the edges column for your score and build a patient
whose values fall on one of them. For example:

- MELD-Na: a patient on dialysis, or a sodium of 118
- qSOFA: a Glasgow score of 14
- Fleischner: a 6 mm subsolid nodule in a patient under 35
- CHA₂DS₂-VASc: a 74-year-old, then a 75-year-old

Compare the three sources.

**Case 3, the nonsense.** Give the tool something no patient has. Both age
bands ticked. A negative creatinine. Every box checked and then every box
unchecked. A blank form. The question is not whether the tool refuses (it
usually will not). The question is whether you can say, before pressing
anything, what it will do, and whether what it does is safe or silent.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example: what to expect, and what to look for" collapse="true"}
**Expected behaviour, not a recorded run.** The two examples below are built
from the failure patterns in @tbl-menu, not from what a particular model
produced on a particular day. Run the prompt yourself and compare.

**CHA₂DS₂-VASc, expected.** The page will usually get the eight point values
right and add them up correctly. That is the easy part. Look instead at three
places. First, the two age boxes. If both
"65–74" and "≥75" can be ticked at once, the page can produce a score of 3
for age, which no patient has. Second, the stroke-risk percentages beside
each score. The page will print a column of numbers with a footnote naming
Lip et al. 2010. But the numbers most tools print come from a different
group of patients [@pmid:22246443], and the two tables disagree. If the
footnote does not say which, that is the version failure. Third, the "female
sex" box. It scored 1 in the 2010 paper and is treated differently by newer
guidelines. A page that scores it without saying which guideline it follows
has chosen for you.

**MELD-Na, expected.** The formula will be right. What tends to be missing
is exactly what the opening scenario depended on. No dialysis field, so
creatinine is never set to 4.0. Values below 1.0 are not raised to it. No
limits on sodium, so a sodium of 118 enters the equation as typed. No check
that the sodium term applies only above the MELD threshold. And if it does
limit sodium, no word on whose limits it uses, the 2008 paper's or the
transplant system's. Ask the page for a patient on dialysis and one with a
sodium of 118, then compare to MDCalc.

Your run will differ from these expectations in both directions. Models
change monthly, and the same prompt produces different code on different
days. The pattern is what to look for. The arithmetic is usually right; the
rules at the edges are where to read.
:::

**Record it.** Copy this into a document. It also answers question 2 of your
[learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd): one time you checked the
AI, how, and what you found.

```
Tool used: ___________________   Model version if shown: ____________
Score built: __________________  Version the tool says it implements: ________

Case            Inputs (invented)         My tool   MDCalc   Paper    Agree?
1 ordinary      _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N
2 edge          _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N
3 nonsense      _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N

Difference or edge failure found ("none" needs the edges you tried):
________________________________________________________________________
Which of the three failures in the table is it: rule / edge / version?
________________________________________________________________________
The one change I would make before letting anyone else use it:
________________________________________________________________________
```

"None found" is a good result, if you can say which edges you tried. It is
still not validation: the tool has been tested on three cases.

**The one sentence.** Write the sentence you would say to a co-intern who
shows you a calculator they built last night. It should contain a verb that
means *compare against something outside the tool*.

### Part C (optional): explain it, then place it (10 minutes)

**The comprehension test.** In four sentences, without opening the code, write
what your tool does for: an ordinary patient, the edge case, the nonsense
case, and a blank form. If you cannot write the fourth sentence, ask the model
"what does the page show when nothing is entered, and why?". Read the answer
against the page, and then write it. This is the test the resident never took.

**Where it sits.** One paragraph. Is your tool, as it is, a study aid or
something a team could rely on? Say why, using the word "banner". Then answer
the four questions from "Four questions before anyone else uses it" for your
tool, and name what would have to change before anyone else used it.

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The chatbot-versus-agent distinction (objective 1) | You can say what the loop adds (acts on real files, observes, repeats, inside permissions) and why a running tool hides errors a reply does not | "An agent is a smarter chatbot" |
| A working tool (objective 2) | Runs in a browser, shows inputs and total, carries the banner, cites the paper and names the version | Runs, but the banner or citation is missing, or the version is unstated |
| Three recorded cases (objective 3) | Each compared against MDCalc *and* the original paper; any difference named and sorted as rule, edge, or version, or, if all agree, the edges you tried listed | "It matched MDCalc" with no edge case tried |
| The one sentence | Contains a verb meaning *compare against an outside source* | "Be careful with it" |
| The comprehension test (Part C, optional) | Four sentences, including the blank form, written before opening the code | The fourth sentence is missing or copied from the model |
| Where it sits (Part C, optional; objective 4) | Says why it is a study aid now, answers the four questions for your tool, and names what would have to change before anyone else used it | "It's not a device because it's just a prototype" |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter. Two specifics. First, go back to the workroom. The
coordinator is on the phone, the team's number is 24, hers is 32, and the
bookmark is on every computer. What do you say to her? What do you say to the
resident who built it? What happens to the bookmark? Second, think of the next
tool you build yourself, or are handed by a colleague. Name the three cases
you will run through it before it touches a decision, and the outside source
each one is compared against. One word is not an answer to either.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- VIBE-HI, the governance framework behind the four questions, with its four
  risk tiers mapped to regulation [@pmid:42564266]; and the
  laboratory-medicine editorial on the illusion of competence
  [@pmid:42695169].
- The clinical-calculation study [@pmid:40097720]: code the model wrote for
  itself helped a little, and calculators built and checked by people helped
  most. Also the cardiology group's technical validation of a
  ChatGPT-built calculator against a registry [@pmid:40462782], which shows
  what your Part B could become.
- Two views of the same practice from inside medicine: an editorial arguing
  it opens biomedical software to everyone [@pmid:40598546], and a
  medical-education piece that built two teaching simulations this way
  [@pmid:40202513].
- The one evaluated medical-education app built by prompting, an ECG tutor
  compared against control sites, with mixed and inconsistent effects on exam
  performance [@doi:10.3390/ai7060223]. Building fast is not the same as
  building something that works.
- Two studies of code written with AI help, both from before current models.
  About 40 percent of programs from an early coding assistant, in
  security-relevant scenarios, had a vulnerability
  [@doi:10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833571]. People using an assistant wrote less
  secure code and were more confident that it was secure
  [@doi:10.1145/3576915.3623157]. Hence the rule in the Do: put nothing in
  your page worth stealing.

**Talks**

- [From Chatbots to Coding Agents](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-06-18-cshl/)
  and [AI Agents for Biomedical Knowledge Work](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-07-28-umihc/),
  the author's slides this chapter's approach comes from; the second has the
  privacy-and-trust section in full.

**If you want to go further**

- The full agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot in an
  editor) need a local install and a terminal, and most need a paid plan. Try
  one after the course, on a project with nothing in it worth stealing.
- Google Colab runs Python notebooks in a browser with a Google account and no
  install. Its built-in agent can run a whole data analysis, start to finish,
  from a prompt. This course's predecessor used it for a public insurance-cost
  dataset. The completed notebook is a good thing to appraise: ask what the
  agent decided without being asked, and what you would want to know before
  believing its R².
